title: Bansuri bamboo flute
summary: The bansuri, called murali in Nepal, is a side-blown flute cut from a single length of bamboo with six finger holes. A player shapes the air with the lips and lifts fingers from the bottom upward to climb a scale, singing folk melodies and long phrases.
howToPlay: Eight lanes stand for the notes of a scale, from the lowest note on the left to the octave on the right.
Above each lane a diagram shows the six finger holes: filled holes are covered, open ones are lifted.
Notes travel toward a line at the bottom; strike the lane just as a note arrives, and let long notes ring.
Begin with the ladder up and down the scale, then play the hill-path tune and the call across the valley.
rules: The scale is seven notes of a major mode plus the octave; pitches follow a fixed root.
Covering all six holes gives the lowest note; lifting fingers from the bottom upward raises it step by step.
A stroke within a hair of the note is perfect, a near one is good, and a missed one scores nothing.
An extra stroke while a song is running costs a few points.
Each song plays twice; three stars need roughly nine notes in ten on time.
heritageNote: Bamboo flutes are played in the hills and valleys of India and Nepal by herders, village singers and concert musicians alike. A flute is cut and tuned to a single key, so players keep a family of lengths.
